Manufacturing and wholesale and retail trade, prime users of transportation services, are shifting to suburban locations, where land is available for single-story industrial plant technology. Oftentimes central city headquarters are preserved, but new production, distribution, and storage facilities are built in outlying areas. This specialization in land use is the result of a "sorting out" process which is directed by land use economic forces. With this rise in specialization, there is a concomitant decline in self-sufficiency, and greater interdependence becomes necessary. Improved communication and transportation networks facilitate coordination of business activity between office and plant locations. Thus, it is modern technological developments which permit a greater degree of commercial integration between city and suburb.
It is the thesis of the Short Haul Committee and other parties opposing an expansion of existing commercial zones
As the scale of urban growth increases, so specialization in the use of urban space becomes essential, and the opportunities for it to occur become greater. But the corollary of land use specialization is interdependence; the various specialized parts of the region become increasingly more intertwined and dependent on each other. The most obvious example of this interdependence is the daily flow of commuters from residential suburbs to jobs in the central cities; but this is just one of a variety of kinds of interaction between the region's different parts. M. YEATES & B. GARNER, THE NORTH AMERICAN CITY 458 (1971).
